Publications/ Overview/ Global Respiratory Virus Activity: Weekly Update N° 595 Global Respiratory Virus Activity: Weekly Update N° 595 Week 36, ending 06 September 2026 16 September 2026 | Emergency situation update Download (5.8 MB) Overview In week 36 2026, globally, influenza positivity was around 10% and SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low. Influenza positivity was at 10% in the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas and tropical areas. Influenza positivity increased to 10% in the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas but there was also a decrease in the reported specimens tested for week 36. RSV positivity also remained low globally. Influenza Globally, influenza detections remained low in week 36 with influenza A viruses detections predominant. In the southern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in some countries in Temperate South America and in single countries in Tropical South America and Eastern Africa. Percent positivity was over 30% in one country in Oceania where a small increase in activity was observed. A small increase in activity was also reported in a single country in Temperate South America. In the northern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in some countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Western Africa, Western, Southern, South-East and Eastern Asia, and in single countries in Tropical South America and Middle and Eastern Africa. Percent positivity was over 30% in some countries in Western Africa and Southern Asia and in a single country in South-East Asia. Increases in activity were observed in some countries in Western, Southern and South-East Asia and in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Northern Europe, Western and Eastern Africa, and Eastern Asia. In the zones with elevated positivity, influenza A(H3N2) was predominant in Western Africa, Eastern Asia and Oceania; influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 was predominant in Eastern Africa, Western, Southern and South-East Asia and influenza B was predominant in Temperate South America. Influenza A and B were codominant in Central America and the Caribbean and Tropical South America. SARS-CoV-2 Globally, SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low across most reporting countries, with elevated positivity (>10%) reported in some countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Northern and South West Europe and Eastern Asia, and in single countries in Tropical South America and Western, Southern and Eastern Asia. Small increases in activity were observed in countries in Northern Europe, and in single countries in Tropical South America, South West Europe and Western, South-East and Eastern Asia. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) RSV positivity was elevated (>10%) in a few countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Temperate South America and in single countries in Western Africa and Southern Asia. Percent positivity was over 30% in a single country in Temperate South America. Increases in activity were observed in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Western Africa and Southern Asia. RSV and influenza activity were both elevated in countries in Temperate South America, Western Africa and Southern Asia. Severity assessment The severity assessments here are reported from countries, areas and territories. Assessments for transmissibility can be reported based on syndromic parameters and/or influenza-specific parameters. In the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as low in a single country; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country. In the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in 14 countries, and low and moderate in single countries; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in nine countries. Influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country in the tropical areas. WHO encourages countries, especially those that have received the multiplex influenza and SARS-CoV-2 reagent kits from GISRS, to conduct integrated surveillance of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 and report epidemiological and laboratory information in a timely manner to established regional and global platforms. The guidance can be found here. Starting with report #501, the Global Respiratory Virus Activity Weekly Update included data from sentinel surveillance and other types of systematically conducted virologic surveillance. Countries, areas, and territories use a variety of approaches to monitor respiratory virus activity and data in this report may vary from surveillance reports posted elsewhere. Analyses stratified by source of surveillance is available through Respimart. Among hospitalized children and adolescents, seasonal influenza is associated with greater clinical burden than COVID-19, including higher rates of intensive care unit (ICU) admission, complications, and antibiotic use, according to study findings published in The Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal. While COVID-19 and influenza generally cause mild illness in children, both infections can result in severe disease requiring hospitalization. Previous pediatric comparisons have produced varying results regarding the relative severity of these infections. Researchers conducted a nationwide prospective surveillance study to characterize differences in epidemiology, clinical presentation, disease severity, and outcomes between children hospitalized with COVID-19 and those hospitalized with influenza. Continued surveillance remains important to monitor changes in the clinical impact of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza in children and to inform vaccination and public health policy. The analysis included patients younger than 18 years hospitalized for more than 24 hours in Switzerland with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 or influenza infection between December 2018 and November 2023. COVID-19 cases were evaluated across periods dominated by wild-type SARS-CoV-2 (T1), Alpha (T2), Delta (T3), and Omicron (T4), while influenza cases were divided into pre-COVID and COVID-era periods. Among 4662 children included in the study, 3132 (67.2%) had SARS-CoV-2 infection and 1530 (32.8%) had influenza. Overall, 45.7% were girls, and more than half were 2 years of age or younger. Age patterns differed significantly by infection and study period (P <.001). Infants represented 32.2% to 46.7% of SARS-CoV-2 admissions across variant periods, whereas influenza admissions more frequently involved toddlers and school-aged children. At least 1 underlying condition was documented in 25.8% of the overall population, with prematurity and neurologic or neuromuscular conditions among the most common. Fever, cough, and rhinitis were common with both infections. The prevalence of fever among children with SARS-CoV-2 declined to 47.3% during the Omicron period, compared with 62.8%, 55.7%, and 64.9% during the wild-type, Alpha, and Delta periods, respectively. Fever occurred in 26.0% of influenza cases during the COVID-era period. Anosmia was limited to SARS-CoV-2 cases and occurred most frequently during the wild-type period (1.2%; P <.001). The researchers reported respiratory distress in 18.1% of children with influenza and 12.6% of those hospitalized during the Omicron period (P =.02). Overall, ICU admission occurred more frequently among children with influenza than among those with SARS-CoV-2 infection (11.4% vs 7.9%; P <.001). Influenza-associated ICU admission rates were 10.5% before the pandemic and 11.8% during the pandemic, while rates across SARS-CoV-2 periods ranged from 5.0% to 10.3%. The use of respiratory support was numerically greater with influenza, although the between-group difference did not reach statistical significance. Children with influenza also experienced significantly more complications (P <.001). The most common complication was lobar pneumonia and affected approximately 20% of children hospitalized with influenza during both influenza periods. Acute respiratory distress syndrome was reported only among patients with influenza and was not observed among those with SARS-CoV-2 infection. Antibiotics were administered to 40.7% of children with influenza compared with 14.4% of those with COVID-19 (P <.001). The most commonly administered antibiotics were amoxicillin-clavulanate, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. Several underlying conditions were independently associated with severe disease, defined as requiring invasive or noninvasive ventilation. Among children with SARS-CoV-2, these included cardiovascular conditions (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 6.37; 95% CI, 3.29-12.35), neurologic or neuromuscular conditions (aOR, 4.64; 95% CI, 2.52-8.51), and other underlying conditions (aOR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.05-3.55). For influenza, severe disease was associated with neurologic or neuromuscular conditions (aOR, 5.70; 95% CI, 3.07-10.59) and respiratory conditions (aOR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.04-4.98). Study limitations include an inability to determine whether infection was the primary reason for every hospitalization, changes in the number of participating hospitals over time, and the use of ventilation requirements to define severe disease. Vaccination data also were not systematically available. “Continued surveillance remains important to monitor changes in the clinical impact of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza in children and to inform vaccination and public health policy,” the researchers concluded. OffOn Stream on FDA approves Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine Moderna was seeking approval for the vaccine's use in adults over 50. ByYouri Benadjaoud, Mary Kekatos, and Eric M. Strauss August 6, 2026, 3:59 AM The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine on Wednesday. The vaccine, mFLUSIVA, is expected to be available for people 50 and older for the 2026-2027 respiratory illness season. "Flu remains a significant public health challenge, and mFLUSIVA provides an important new option for America's seniors. This approval also reflects the ongoing potential of our mRNA platform to help address important public health challenges through continued scientific innovation," Stéphane Bancel, Chief Executive Officer of Moderna, said in a statement. In this Dec. 15, 2020, file photo, the Moderna, Inc. headquarters is shown in Cambridge, Mass. Elise Amendola/AP, FILE In a clinical trial for people aged 50 to 64, the mRNA vaccine led to 27% fewer confirmed flu cases than the current standard vaccine. The safety profile for Moderna’s vaccine and the current standard was about the same, but more people taking the mRNA vaccine reported side effects; those were mostly mild and lasted two days or less. For people 65 and older, a high-dose vaccine is currently recommended. Moderna said it will keep data this winter on how mFlusiva does compared to the current high-dose vaccine and submit that to the FDA to see if the vaccine remains approved for that population. Earlier this year, the FDA announced it would not review Moderna's application for the vaccine. However, the agency backtracked and agreed to review the shot after Moderna promised to conduct another study after the shot became available on the market. The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine on Wednesday. Health UAE health ministry urges annual flu vaccination as seasonal influenza can lead to complications Ministry identifies six high-risk groups and says vaccination remains the most effective protection against seasonal influenza By Emad El-Din Khalil Published: 2026-09-21T08:25:00+04:00 3 min read The ministry stressed that annual vaccination and preventive measures remain the most effective way to reduce the impact of seasonal influenza and its complications. Dubai: The Ministry of Health and Prevention (MoHAP) has urged residents to receive the seasonal influenza vaccine, warning that the disease, which often begins with symptoms such as fever, cough, fatigue and muscle aches, can develop into a serious illness requiring hospitalisation, particularly among vulnerable groups. The ministry said influenza vaccination can provide up to 90 per cent protection against clinical illness in healthy adults and remains the most effective way to prevent infection, reduce the severity of illness and lower the risk of hospitalisation. Acute respiratory infection The ministry explained that seasonal influenza is an acute infectious respiratory disease caused by influenza viruses, which circulate during specific seasons, particularly in winter. Influenza viruses belong to the Orthomyxoviridae family and are classified into three types: A, B and C. MoHAP noted that the influenza vaccine is an inactivated vaccine containing virus particles that cannot cause the disease. The vaccine is available to everyone aged six months and above through government and private healthcare facilities across the UAE. Symptoms and transmission The ministry said seasonal influenza symptoms can range from mild to severe and generally resolve within a week without medical intervention. However, in some cases, the disease can lead to serious complications requiring hospitalisation. Symptoms include: Fever Headache Fatigue Cough Muscle aches Joint pain Sore throat Runny nose Vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly in children The incubation period is approximately two days and may range from one to four days. Influenza is transmitted through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks. It can also spread indirectly through contact with contaminated hands, objects or surfaces, followed by touching the mouth, nose or eyes. Six high-risk groups The ministry identified six groups that are most vulnerable to influenza and its complications: Pregnant women at any stage of pregnancy Children under five years old Elderly people Healthcare workers Individuals with chronic medical conditions, including heart, lung, kidney, liver and blood diseases People with weakened or compromised immune systems MoHAP outlined seven key preventive measures: Receiving the influenza vaccine Following proper cough and sneeze etiquette Avoiding close contact with infected individuals Regularly cleaning and disinfecting frequently used surfaces and objects Washing and sanitising hands regularly Staying away from others when symptoms develop Avoiding touching the eyes, nose and mouth The ministry recommended receiving the vaccine annually in September or early winter before the start of the flu season. However, it stressed that vaccination remains beneficial even if received later, as influenza activity can continue for several months. It noted that the body requires approximately two weeks after vaccination to develop protection. Safe and effective vaccine The ministry emphasised that the influenza vaccine has been administered to millions of people worldwide for more than 60 years and has a strong safety record. According to the ministry, side effects are generally mild and resolve on their own within a few days. Global impact The ministry said seasonal influenza affects approximately 5 to 10 per cent of adults and 20 to 30 per cent of children worldwide each year. Globally, influenza results in an estimated three to five million severe cases annually and causes between 290,000 and 650,000 deaths from respiratory complications. While most people recover without complications, the ministry warned that the disease can lead to serious health consequences, particularly among high-risk groups. It also noted that every influenza season differs from the previous one and may affect people in different ways. Benefits of vaccination The ministry cited studies showing that influenza vaccination: Reduces the severity of illness in infected individuals Reduces hospital admissions among older adults by 25 to 39 per cent Reduces overall mortality by 39 to 75 per cent Provides approximately 70 to 90 per cent protection against clinical illness in healthy adults The ministry also highlighted five key benefits of vaccination: Protecting individuals from influenza infection Reducing the risk of hospitalisation Reducing the severity of illness Protecting pregnant women during and after pregnancy Protecting infants during their first months of life and contributing to community protection, particularly for vulnerable groups The ministry stressed that annual vaccination and preventive measures remain the most effective way to reduce the impact of seasonal influenza and its complications

Share Article Aktivitas influenza di Indonesia menunjukkan peningkatan dalam beberapa pekan terakhir. Data terbaru Kementerian Kesehatan (Kemenkes) RI memperlihatkan A(H1N1)pdm09 menjadi subtipe influenza yang paling banyak ditemukan dalam pemeriksaan laboratorium. Dalam Laporan Pengawasan Kasus Influenza dan COVID-19 yang diperbarui pada 19 September 2026, Kemenkes mencatat proporsi spesimen positif influenza pada minggu ke-36 meningkat menjadi 46 persen, dari 35 persen pada minggu sebelumnya. Catatan penting: positivity rate 46 persen merupakan proporsi hasil positif di antara spesimen yang masuk ke sistem surveilans dan diperiksa. Table of Content 1. A(H1N1)pdm09 dominan 2. Pasien influenza yang dirawat di rumah sakit juga meningkat 3. Kasus paling banyak ditemukan pada anak kecil 4. Meski naik, tetapi aktivitas influenza masih dikategorikan rendah 5. Strain influenza yang dominan bisa berubah 1. A(H1N1)pdm09 dominan Pada minggu ke-36, sebanyak 185 spesimen diperiksa dan 86 di antaranya positif influenza. Dari kasus positif tersebut: 76 merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09 (88 persen) 8 merupakan A(H3N2) 2 merupakan influenza B/Victoria Dominasi serupa juga terlihat pada surveilans pelayanan kesehatan primer. Dari 122 spesimen yang diperiksa pada minggu ke-36, 60 positif influenza. Sebanyak 49 merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09, sementara empat A(H3), satu influenza B/Victoria, dan 6 belum ditentukan subtipenya. 2. Pasien influenza yang dirawat di rumah sakit juga meningkat Peningkatan juga terlihat pada jaringan rumah sakit sentinel. Kemenkes melaporkan bahwa proporsi kasus influenza positif di rumah sakit meningkat menjadi 31,7 persen dari 20,4 persen pada minggu sebelumnya. Dari 63 pasien yang dirawat dan diperiksa pada minggu ke-36, 20 positif influenza. Sebanyak 16 kasus merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09, tiga A(H3), dan satu influenza B/Victoria. Namun, tidak ada pasien influenza positif yang membutuhkan perawatan ICU pada minggu itu. 3. Kasus paling banyak ditemukan pada anak kecil ilustrasi influenza A (magnific.com/benzoix) Dalam data surveilans laboratorium, 42 persen kasus influenza yang terdeteksi berasal dari kelompok usia 0–4 tahun. Pada data rawat inap, Kemenkes juga mencatat kasus influenza paling banyak ditemukan pada kelompok usia 0–4 tahun. Anak kecil memang termasuk kelompok yang lebih mudah terkena influenza dan lebih berisiko mengalami komplikasi dibandingkan anak yang lebih besar atau orang dewasa sehat. Sistem imun mereka masih membangun pengalaman terhadap berbagai virus influenza, sementara lingkungan seperti daycare dan sekolah juga meningkatkan peluang paparan. 4. Meski naik, tetapi aktivitas influenza masih dikategorikan rendah Walaupun angka positivity rate meningkat, tetapi Kemenkes menyebut tingkat aktivitas influenza saat ini masih berada dalam kategori rendah dan masih sesuai dengan pola musiman influenza di Indonesia. Penilaian tersebut menggunakan indikator surveilans yang lebih luas, bukan cuma jumlah hasil positif dalam satu minggu. 5. Strain influenza yang dominan bisa berubah Virus influenza yang paling banyak beredar tidak selalu sama sepanjang tahun. Komposisi A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3), dan influenza B berubah-ubah sepanjang 2025–2026. Pada beberapa periode H3 lebih banyak ditemukan, sedangkan menjelang September 2026 proporsi H1N1pdm09 meningkat tajam. Perubahan seperti ini merupakan bagian dari pola epidemiologi influenza. Kekebalan masyarakat, karakter virus yang sedang beredar, musim, mobilitas, dan berbagai faktor lingkungan dapat ikut memengaruhi subtipe mana yang lebih banyak ditemukan pada suatu periode. Data terbaru mingguan Kemenkes ini menunjukkan bahwa aktivitas influenza sedang meningkat dan A(H1N1)pdm09 menjadi subtipe yang mendominasi, tetapi situasi secara keseluruhan masih berada dalam kategori aktivitas rendah. Show original What are the differences between influenza medications? A pharmacist explains 3 treatments used for children 9 ゆっこ│4児のママ薬剤師×保育士 2026年9月20日 16:22 Hello. I am Yukko, a pharmacist and childcare worker who is a mother of four. This year, the influenza season has started earlier than usual. In 2026, the start of the seasonal influenza season was announced on August 28th. This is reportedly the second earliest start since the current infectious disease surveillance system began in 1999. "It's still hot, but influenza is already here?" Many of you may be surprised by this. As the seasons progress into autumn and winter, children may have more opportunities to catch influenza. Therefore, this time, I will summarize the characteristics of influenza treatments often used for children, Oseltamivir, Xofluza, and Inavir from a pharmacist's perspective. *This article is based on public documents and package inserts as of September 2026. Please follow the instructions of your doctor or pharmacist regarding actual treatment. Are anti-influenza drugs always necessary? First, it is important to know that you do not always have to use anti-influenza drugs when you have influenza that. Anti-influenza drugs are expected to shorten the duration of fever by about 1 to 2 days if started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Doctors decide whether to use them by considering symptoms, age, and the risk of severe illness. Oseltamivir You might be more familiar with the name "Tamiflu." It is an oral medication, and it is basically used for 5 days for treatment. Dry syrup is sometimes used for children. Here, the "taste" of children's medicine is surprisingly important. Towa Pharmaceutical's Oseltamivir DS 3% "Towa" is designed with a banana flavor. It is also formulated to reduce the bitterness of the medicine, making it as easy as possible for children to take. On the other hand, side effects such as vomiting are known to occur with oseltamivir. If the child vomits after taking it, do not decide on your own to give them another dose; instead, inform your doctor or pharmacist about how long after taking the medicine the vomiting occurred and consult them. Xofluza A major feature of Xofluza is that treatment is basically completed with a single dose . It comes in tablets and granules, and the 2% granule packet is 10mg per packet. Also, the granules are strawberry flavored🍓. However, you may feel a bitter taste if it is kept in the mouth for a while. Oseltamivir is banana-flavored, and Xofluza granules are strawberry-flavored. Children's medicines are designed with various considerations for taste. Another feature of Xofluza is that the half-life of its active metabolite is long. On the other hand, side effects related to bleeding have been reported, and nosebleeds may occur. This does not mean that you will definitely have a nosebleed if you take it, but if you notice any concerning bleeding, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Also, because it is a single-dose medication, consult your doctor or pharmacist if the child vomits after taking it. The response will be determined based on the time and circumstances of the vomiting, but instead of taking Xofluza again, treatment with another anti-influenza drug, such as oseltamivir or Inavir, may be selected. Inavir Inavir is not an oral medication, but an inhalant. A key feature of this treatment is that it is used for only one day. However, with children, there is often the concern of, "Are they inhaling it properly?" At pharmacies and similar locations, practice devices are sometimes used to practice inhalation. There are also types that make a sound when inhaled with the necessary force, and the sound serves as a benchmark to confirm whether the child has the strength required for inhalation. Also, the irritation during inhalation can sometimes cause coughing or nausea. "They threw up after inhaling!" Even in such cases, since Inavir is an inhalant, you generally do not need to worry that "the medicine came out because they vomited," as you would with an oral medication. If you are worried or are unsure if the inhalation was successful, consult your doctor or pharmacist. And another thing to be aware of is lactose. Inavir uses lactose hydrate, and that lactose contains milk protein as an impurity. Therefore, caution is required if there is a history of hypersensitivity to dairy products. If you have ever had allergic symptoms from milk or dairy products, please inform your doctor or pharmacist when it is prescribed. Features of each of the 3 medications To summarize briefly: Oseltamivir → Oral medication. Used for 5 days. Banana-flavored products available. Watch for vomiting, etc. Xofluza → Oral medication. Finished in one dose. Granules are strawberry-flavored. Watch for bleeding. Inavir → Inhalant. Used for only one day. The key is whether they can inhale it. Also watch for hypersensitivity to dairy products. Rather than saying "which medicine is the best," whether the child can use it properly This perspective is also important. Be careful beyond just medication for the first two days With influenza, you also need to be aware of abnormal behavior in children. Abnormal behavior has been reported even when anti-influenza drugs are not used, and it has been observed regardless of the type of medication or whether it was taken. Therefore, a causal relationship between abnormal behavior and anti-influenza drugs has not been established. Since it often occurs within two days of the onset of fever, when a child has influenza, do not leave them alone for the first two days, regardless of whether they are taking medication or not. This is also a point to keep in mind. The taste of the medicine, the dosage form, how to take it, and whether it can be inhaled. When using medicine for children, these "little differences" are very important. "Will my child be able to take this medicine?" "Will they be able to inhale it?" "They threw it up, will they be okay?" In such cases, please consult your doctor or pharmacist. As a pharmacist, I hope to help reduce the burden on children and the family members caring for them, even if just a little. A new review published in Virology Journal examines one of the least explored dimensions of this pathogen: the role of human immunogenetics in shaping who falls ill, how severely, and how well they respond to vaccination. The work, led by Ghayyas Ud Din and Hizbullah Khan, who share first authorship, alongside colleagues at institutions including the Shanghai Institute of Immunity and Infection and Guangdong Medical University, offers a careful stocktaking of what is known, what is merely inferred, and where the field must go next. Unlike influenza A, influenza B virus lacks a broad animal reservoir and, with it, the pandemic potential that makes influenza A a constant global security concern. But the absence of pandemic risk has never equated to clinical irrelevance. Influenza B virus drives substantial morbidity in seasonal epidemics, and its two historically circulating lineages, B/Victoria and B/Yamagata, have followed strikingly different trajectories in recent years. Surveillance has documented no confirmed naturally circulating B/Yamagata-lineage viruses since March 2020, a development widely linked to the intense non-pharmaceutical interventions of the COVID-19 pandemic era. Current influenza B activity is now overwhelmingly attributable to B/Victoria-lineage viruses, a shift with real consequences for vaccine composition and the interpretation of vaccine effectiveness studies. The central premise of the review is that the host genome may help explain a persistent puzzle: why individuals exposed to the same virus, and receiving the same vaccine, experience markedly different outcomes. Variation in genes governing antigen presentation, innate viral sensing, interferon signaling, and host dependency or restriction factors could plausibly generate heterogeneity in susceptibility, disease severity, cross-lineage immunity, and responsiveness to immunization. This framework draws on decades of immunogenetic research in influenza A and in broader antiviral biology, but the authors stress a crucial caveat: much of what has been proposed for influenza B rests on inference rather than on direct, influenza B virus-specific human data. Discover more genetic Biological Sciences genetics Parasites & Parasitic Diseases Infectious Diseases At the heart of the immunogenetic hypothesis lies the human leukocyte antigen system, the protein complex responsible for presenting viral peptide fragments to T cells. Differences in HLA alleles can alter which viral epitopes are displayed, how strongly T cells respond, and consequently how efficiently an infected or vaccinated individual clears virus or mounts protective memory. For influenza A, associations between specific HLA variants and outcomes such as infection risk, severity, and antibody titers after vaccination have been reported across multiple populations. Extending these findings to influenza B is not straightforward, however, because the two virus types differ in their evolutionary dynamics, transmission patterns, and the antigenic landscape they present to the immune system. Epitope repertoires are not interchangeable, and a genetic variant that enhances clearance of one influenza type may have little or no measurable effect on the other. Beyond antigen presentation, the review considers the innate immune machinery that first detects invading influenza viruses. Pattern recognition receptors such as the toll-like receptors and RIG-I-like receptors sense viral RNA and trigger signaling cascades that culminate in interferon production. Genetic polymorphisms in these sensors and in the downstream interferon pathway can modulate the vigor of the early antiviral response, potentially determining whether an infection is contained quickly or gains a foothold. Similarly, host dependency factors that the virus requires for entry, replication, and assembly, along with restriction factors that actively inhibit viral replication, represent additional layers where inherited variation could shape susceptibility. Each of these domains offers a plausible mechanistic route by which host genotype could influence influenza B outcomes, yet the authors find that direct evidence in the influenza B context remains sparse and fragmentary. When it comes to vaccine response, the review is similarly measured. The best-supported determinants of influenza vaccine performance, the authors conclude, are not genetic at all. Antigenic match between vaccine strains and circulating viruses, the continuous process of antigenic drift that erodes that match over time, the age of the vaccinee, prior exposure history, and baseline immunity stand out as the factors with the strongest evidentiary grounding. These non-genetic determinants have been repeatedly validated across seasons and populations, and they explain a considerable portion of the year-to-year variability in vaccine effectiveness. Genetic predictors specific to influenza B, by contrast, remain incompletely defined, and no validated host-genetic biomarker currently exists to guide vaccination decisions for this virus. This asymmetry between well-established extrinsic factors and poorly characterized intrinsic ones is not merely an academic gap. Predictive models of influenza B immune control and vaccine performance are limited by the absence of genotype-linked outcome data. Without large, well-phenotyped cohorts in which host genotype, immune phenotyping, and lineage-resolved virologic outcomes are collected together, the field cannot distinguish genuine genetic effects from confounding by age, prior exposure, or antigenic distance. The authors argue that such integrated studies represent the most important priority for future research, and they outline a research agenda built around linking these data streams in a single analytical framework. Discover more Genes genes Health Conditions Genetic Medical Literature & Resources The disappearance of the B/Yamagata lineage adds an unusual wrinkle to this agenda. With no naturally circulating Yamagata viruses detected for years, vaccine components targeting that lineage have become biologically obsolete, and regulatory and advisory bodies have been reconsidering the composition of seasonal vaccines, including the transition from quadrivalent to trivalent formulations. For immunogenetic studies, the loss of a circulating lineage complicates the interpretation of historical cross-lineage immunity data and underscores the need for lineage-resolved outcome measures in future cohorts. Any genetic association study conducted today will, in practice, be measuring responses against B/Victoria viruses, and generalizing those findings to influenza B as a whole carries inherent uncertainty. Population-specific variation presents another challenge. Immunogenetic associations identified in one ancestry or geographic setting frequently fail to replicate elsewhere, reflecting both genuine differences in allele frequencies and differences in study design, exposure patterns, and co-circulating pathogens. The international composition of the review team, spanning institutions in China, Pakistan, and Uzbekistan, reflects a growing recognition that influenza B research must extend beyond the settings where it has traditionally been studied. Building the evidence base for immunogenetic determinants will require multi-center collaborations with standardized genotyping platforms, harmonized immune phenotyping protocols, and consistent definitions of susceptibility, severity, and vaccine response. The review, which received support from the Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation and the Dongguan Science and Technology of Social Development Program, ultimately delivers a message of disciplined optimism. The biological logic connecting host genetic variation to influenza B outcomes is sound, and the methodological tools needed to test it, from affordable genome sequencing to sophisticated immune profiling, are now widely available. What is missing is the concerted, influenza B-specific data collection that would convert plausible mechanisms into clinically actionable knowledge. Until that work is done, antigenic match, age, and exposure history will remain the most reliable predictors of how influenza B behaves in populations, while the genome’s contribution waits to be quantified. Show original Out-of-season Influenza: The Difficulty of Answering 'When Can I Return to Work?' 1 ねりごま 2026年9月19日 08:57 Influenza has already entered a period of prevalence. At my workplace, we are busy responding to cases, such as diagnosing influenza A in outpatients and implementing infection control measures on one floor to curb the spread. This August onset is the second earliest since the Infectious Diseases Control Law was enacted in 1999. They say it's the second earliest, but do you know when the first was? It was 2009. It might be a story from long ago that many people don't know, but at the time it was called novel influenza. And this year, the virus said to be at the center of the outbreak is named A(H1N1)pdm09*. It is the same lineage as the virus that emerged in 2009. The WHO declared the end of the pandemic in August 2010, and since then, it has been treated as seasonal influenza. Seventeen years after its emergence in 2009, it continues to circulate every year as the same virus, while changing its appearance little by little. Even though it is the same virus, there is the 'novel' one that was considered a threat and the 'seasonal' one that is an annual occurrence. What separates the two? What separates them is 'the relationship between the virus and the immunity of the host'. The difference between novel and seasonal is not determined by the virus alone. It is determined by the relationship. In hospitals, too, there are events regarding influenza that are determined by relationships. Three things you receive at the hospital When diagnosed with influenza, you are given several things. Here, I will divide them into three: medication, documentation, and instructions on when you can return to school/work. I am on the side that hands these three things out. Those of us on the giving side actually think about what and how we should hand them over. Is it really necessary? How much should we explain? It is painful to listen to a long explanation when you are feverish and feeling sluggish, isn't it? "Medication" WHO guidelines do not target influenza treatment for healthy individuals without risks. In Western countries, the principle is to use nothing but antipyretics for healthy people, and even those are mainly for the purpose of relieving pain rather than for treatment. The US CDC also recommends antiviral drugs only for those at high risk of severe illness, such as the elderly or those with underlying conditions. Japan prescribes them widely, even to healthy adults and children. I want to go back to work quickly, I want the peace of mind that comes with getting medicine, other doctors have prescribed it for me. There is also the aspect that it is faster to prescribe than to carefully explain why you are not. It is not purely determined by medical reasons. Whether or not to prescribe medication is determined by the relationship with the patient. "Documentation" Medical certificates or certificates of recovery. In the Q&A issued by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, it is stated that submission of a certificate of recovery is unnecessary. It even goes so far as to say that it is undesirable for workplaces to require employees to submit certificates of recovery or negative test results. The same applies when returning to school. Workplaces also request them out of good intentions, saying, 'It wouldn't do to infect others.' --Those with less medical knowledge are institutionalizing based on worry. Patients request them because 'I can't work unless I submit it.' --In some cases, it becomes a significant expense out of pocket. Medical providers write them because 'I was asked to write one.' --Sometimes I ask, 'Wouldn't a receipt serve as proof of the visit?' Whether or not to issue documentation is determined not just by the body, but by the relationship with the workplace and living environment. To begin with, what constitutes a recovery? Is it the person's body, the shedding of the virus, or the risk of infecting others? I issue the standard form while harboring these vague feelings. "Instructions" For schools, there are standards under the School Health and Safety Act. The rules state that attendance is suspended until 5 days have passed since the onset and 2 days (3 days for infants) have passed since the fever subsided. This applies up to university level, so this applies to students even if they are adults. There is no uniform statutory number of days for returning to the workplace. Seasonal influenza is classified as a Category V infectious disease under the Infectious Diseases Control Law and is not subject to work restrictions. In other words, there is no legally mandated period for suspension from work. If your company has work regulations, you must follow them, but those are rules specific to each company. Incidentally, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare explains that since the virus is shed from the day before onset to 3–7 days after onset, one should refrain from going out while shedding the virus. This is not a rule divided by a specific number of days, and the way it is counted differs from school standards. Therefore, when asked 'When can I go back to work?', the basis for the answer changes depending on the person. For a student, it is based on legal requirements. For a working person, it depends on company rules and the individual's condition. I do explain it by saying something like, 'According to school attendance suspension standards...', though. 'I have opportunities to interact with elderly people; until when should I avoid seeing them?'... There is no absolute, clear-cut standard for that person. How long one must stay at home and alone is determined by one's relationships with those around them. The patient's perspective I believe the reasons for coming to the hospital also vary. Physical discomfort, fear of the illness becoming severe, not wanting to infect family members. And being told by a school or workplace to see a doctor. There is also the desire to be reassured by getting a clear diagnosis. Just knowing what the illness is can be a slight relief. Coming to the hospital for such different reasons, three things are returned for various reasons. All of that is determined by the relationship between the patient, the hospital, and society. Where do the reasons become invisible? On the side giving the information, different grounds are handled at once. Is it medicine, anxiety, legal requirements, or social circumstances? What is given is determined by the relationship with the situation you are in. But when it is received, it is all bundled together. When given together, it is easy for even the grounds to look the same. If you or your family are told at the hospital that it is influenza, I would like you to take a moment to re-examine the three things you were given. For what reason were they given? Medicine, society, or custom? What you received does not change. But I think the meaning of the explanation received looks a little different when you think about where the information came from, rather than just accepting it because 'it was given to you'. The virus that shocked the world 17 years ago is now called seasonal. The virus remains the same in its lineage; what has changed is the side receiving it. And the same thing is happening in the examination room. It is not just the name of the disease that determines what is given. ※A(H1N1)pdm09... An influenza virus that emerged in 2009 and caused a global pandemic. It currently circulates every year as one of the seasonal influenza strains. 投稿 ログイン 会員登録 SYSTEM NOTICE Auto translation by AI. Be sure, accuracy, nuances and authorial intent may not be fully reflected. Show original Influenza B arrives after the New Year. Does the vaccine given in September still work by then? ひろつ内科クリニック院長 / Dr.Hirotsu 2026年9月17日 10:58 “I heard that Influenza B becomes prevalent in the latter half of winter. Does the vaccine I received in September still work by then?” Since we started vaccinations, I have begun to receive questions like this. I think it is a good question. And, to answer honestly, there is no clean answer. I will write three things first. It is true according to data that the detection of Influenza B has been skewed toward the period after the New Year for the past several seasons. However, whether the effect of a vaccine given in September lasts until that time has not been settled yet. And, I do not make the decision to delay vaccination based on the fact that it is not settled. It is true that Influenza B is skewed toward the latter part of the season Looking at the weekly detection reports from the National Institute of Health Crisis Management, of the 3,962 cases of Influenza B detected last season (2025/26), 94.7% were after the New Year. 90.4% occurred in January to March alone. The peaks were also 13 weeks apart, with A(H3) in the 47th week of 2025 and B/Victoria in the 7th week of 2026. The same pattern appeared in 2023/24 and 2024/25. However, when it comes and how much of it comes are different things. The proportion of Influenza B in the entire season fluctuates from 2.3% to 45.0% depending on the year. In 2022/23, it was 2.3%, with only 91 cases. There are years when it comes and years when it hardly comes at all. The premise has also changed. The B/Yamagata lineage has not been detected in Japan for six consecutive seasons since 2020/21. Japanese vaccines have also become trivalent since 2025/26, so now when we say “Influenza B,” we mean B/Victoria. The point is not whether to get two doses The dosage in the package insert is one dose for those 13 and older, or two doses at an interval of about 1 to 4 weeks. The two-dose vaccination described is for this interval, and a method of getting one dose in September and another several months later is not written. As far as I have confirmed, there are no public institutions that recommend additional vaccinations for adults during the season. Therefore, the point is not whether to get two doses. It is how long the effect of one dose lasts. I would not recommend that those who were vaccinated in September get vaccinated again for the latter half of winter. I think it is fine to consider that as completed. That “how long” has not been settled There is a 2025 report that analyzed the time after 5 months from vaccination in healthy adults aged 18 to 65. I will write how to read the numbers first. The following is an indicator (adjusted odds ratio) showing that the lower the value is below 1, the fewer infections there were among vaccinated people, and if the range shown together (95% confidence interval) straddles 1, it means “it could not be determined whether there was a difference or not.” A(H1N1)pdm09 was 0.66, with a range of 0.51 to 0.87. It does not straddle 1. It is a value that can be read as protection remaining. On the other hand, Influenza B was 0.75, with a range of 0.49 to 1.16. It straddles 1. Even though the value itself points toward protection, it cannot be stated definitively. This is a point that is easily misunderstood. “Not significant” does not mean “no effect.” It means it could not be determined within the scope of this analysis. For the same reason, there is no basis to say definitively that “Influenza B will also last without problems.” The research itself is divided There are reports that detected a decline and reports that found no evidence, both exist. On the side of a decline, a 2016 report showed effectiveness against Influenza B was 70.7% (51.3–82.4) 44 days after vaccination, and 21.4% (−57.4–60.8) at the end of the season. However, since the range at the end of the season straddles 0, it cannot be read as “it dropped to 21%.” In a 2018 report, the amount of change for Influenza B was −19 (−33 to −6). On the side of no decline, an analysis of a total of 210,000 cases in the UK stated that “there was evidence of a decline for Influenza A, but no evidence of a decline for Influenza B.” A 2025 report looking at hospitalizations in the US showed Influenza B at 67% (35–84), which was higher than the 36% (21–48) for A(H1N1). A 2026 review summarizing 49 studies states that attenuation was observed more consistently for Influenza A, especially A(H3N2), than for Influenza B. In short, neither the claim that "Type B protection wanes quickly" nor "Type B protection does not wane" can be supported by the current evidence. Not only is the magnitude of the conclusion unclear, but the findings are not even consistent in direction. To be clear, the reason this remains unresolved is only a matter of how much protection against Type B remains in the latter half of winter. It does not mean that getting vaccinated in September was a waste, and the protection against the currently circulating Type A has been working since the moment you received the shot. I will leave what is unknown as it is. It has not been determined whether the observed decline is truly a waning of immunity or a bias stemming from research methodology. Many of the studies cited here include periods when the B/Yamagata lineage was still circulating. There is no data available that looks specifically at B/Victoria by days elapsed since vaccination. There is no data in Japan on Type B stratified by days elapsed since vaccination. All of it comes from overseas reports, and we are applying that to the situation in Japan. None of the reports cited so far are randomized controlled trials that directly verified whether the results for Type B change between September and November vaccinations. We do not even know if Type B will arrive this season. Domestic detections this season (weeks 32-36) include 56 cases of A(H1N1)pdm09, 1 case of A(H3), and 0 cases of Type B. Since there is no prediction that can provide a probability, I will not write down any numbers. Even so, I will not delay it. In Japan, the guideline for seasonal influenza vaccination is to start from mid-to-late October and finish by early December. Our clinic began vaccinations on September 12th to accommodate those who wish to be vaccinated at this time, and this does not replace the guidelines. Furthermore, regarding the question of "Why not wait until November?": A 2020 modeling study estimated that if vaccinations were delayed until October, more than 14% of those who had previously been vaccinated in August or September would miss their chance, potentially leading to an increase in hospitalizations. The decision to delay is conditional on the assumption that those who delay will actually come back to get vaccinated; if the rate of missed vaccinations exceeds a certain level, it could result in a net loss. This is based on a US modeling study, not a Japanese estimate. I will provide overseas recommendations as supplementary information. They do not replace Japanese recommendations. The US Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices does not recommend vaccination in July and August, but considers September and October to be ideal times. Canada's recommendations for this season also state that early autumn vaccination provides protection for the majority of the season. What is currently being detected is A(H1N1)pdm09. As mentioned in the previous review, waning is more consistently observed with Type A, so this does not mean there is no need to worry about Type A. Even so, I do not delay preparations for an ongoing outbreak based on the unresolved status of Type B. What you can do now for the latter half of winter If you develop a fever after the New Year, please consult us rather than deciding for yourself that it is not influenza because you were vaccinated. Having the whole family vaccinated is one approach. A randomized controlled trial involving a community overseas reported that vaccinating children indirectly reduced infections among unvaccinated people around them. While it has not been confirmed that the same result will occur in a household, it is one way of thinking about it. Hand washing and ventilation should be continued through the latter half of winter. I realize that writing that something is unknown when it is unknown makes for an unsatisfying article. Nevertheless, since there is not enough evidence to write about this definitively, I will leave it as it is. The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA) said Wednesday it revised the schedule for the 2026-2027 seasonal influenza National Immunization Program (NIP) after issuing a flu epidemic advisory last Friday. The agency said it adjusted the schedule after considering the current outbreak and its outlook, vaccine supplies, medical needs and healthcare providers’ readiness. The decision followed a review by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and consultations with medical groups and local governments. Influenza has recently spread rapidly, particularly among school-age children and younger age groups. (Credit: Getty Images) In the 36th week of this year, the rate of influenza-like illness was highest among children aged 7-12, at 75.1 cases per 1,000 outpatients. The rate was 49.8 among children aged 1-6, 31.3 among those aged 13-18 and 24.0 among infants under age 1. Although the rate among people aged 65 and older was relatively low at 8.8 per 1,000 outpatients, the age group accounted for 60.0 percent of all patients hospitalized with influenza. Children's vaccinations moved up to next Monday, elderly schedule advanced by 3-6 days Under the revised schedule, NIP influenza vaccinations for children aged six months to 14 years will begin next Monday. Children requiring one dose were already scheduled to begin vaccination next Monday. Those requiring two doses, however, had originally been scheduled to start Sept. 28. The government moved their start date forward by one week to next Monday. Vaccinations for pregnant women will begin next Monday as originally scheduled. The vaccination schedule for older adults will also be moved forward. Vaccinations for people aged 75 and older will begin Oct. 6, six days earlier than the previous Oct. 12 start date. Those aged 70-74 will begin Oct. 12 instead of Oct. 15, while those aged 65-69 will start Oct. 15 instead of Oct. 19. High-risk groups, including immunocompromised people, can receive vaccinations from Oct. 6 after consulting healthcare professionals, regardless of their age-group schedule. Long-term care hospitals and facilities will not have a separate vaccination start date and may begin administering shots as soon as vaccines are supplied. NIP secures 12.33 million doses, but private supplies remain tight The KDCA said it expects no disruption to the national vaccination program despite the accelerated schedule. The agency has secured about 12.33 million influenza vaccine doses for the 2026-2027 NIP season and plans to distribute them gradually to healthcare providers in line with the revised schedule. Overall vaccine supplies, however, are tighter than in previous years. All three strains recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for this season’s Northern Hemisphere influenza vaccines — influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and B/Victoria lineage strains — were changed. Production yields declined as manufacturers worked to optimize cultivation and manufacturing processes for the new strains, reducing Korea’s total supply of domestically produced and imported vaccines by about 4 million doses from last year. The KDCA said it worked with vaccine manufacturers and importers to secure an additional 370,000 doses for private-sector vaccinations. Still, it acknowledged that private-market supplies remain tighter than in previous years. Domestic production and distribution schedules were also affected because the WHO supplied the reference standard for the influenza B component needed for vaccine quality testing about a month later than last season. The KDCA and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety advanced lot-release approvals by about two weeks from the original schedule, but supplying sufficient quantities before the NIP begins remains challenging. The KDCA plans to review vaccine supply conditions weekly with manufacturers, importers, distributors and the medical community while pursuing additional production and imports. “We adjusted the vaccination schedule in response to the early issuance of the influenza epidemic advisory after reviewing vaccine supply conditions and available quantities and taking into account feedback from experts and those in the field,” KDCA Commissioner Lim Seung-kwan said. Seasonal influenza in Japan typically begins to appear around November and peaks in January or February, but this year it started appearing in late August, and the number of infections has been increasing since entering September. I work at a hospital in Sumida Ward, Tokyo, and since last week, about half of the patients with fevers have had influenza A. Flu season is late and cases are up Published: September 21, 2026 4:09pm EDT The weather is warming up and the hay fever season has begun, but more people are experiencing cases of influenza than expected for spring. In the two weeks to September 6, flu cases were up 27% on the previous two weeks. And case numbers are rising. How is this year’s flu season different? This year, surveillance systems based in laboratories, data from members of the community, GPs and hospitals all suggest influenza activity has been lower than in previous years for most of the year. But influenza case numbers have increased since mid-August. 2026 influenza notifications by state and territory. NIDSS So far, the majority of influenza cases have been due to the H3N2 subtype of influenza A, although some H1N1 and influenza B have also been reported. The H3N2 subtype has mostly been due to the “super K” strain that was associated with a late surge of cases in 2025. This strain seemed to be more transmissible than usual, although it didn’t cause more severe disease. There are also some differences in activity in different parts of Australia. New South Wales and Western Australia both had an increase in influenza activity from late June that was not seen in other other states and territories. What is the usual pattern of influenza in Australia? Since the COVID pandemic, influenza epidemiology has been more unpredictable than usual. Before the pandemic, influenza cases usually started to rise in June-July and peaked in August, falling to lower levels by late October. During the pandemic, influenza activity was essentially absent for 2020 and 2021, but resumed with the re-opening of international borders and relaxation of public health measures in 2022. The influenza seasons in 2022 and 2023 were unusually early, peaking in late June. Last year was also unusual, with an initial peak in mid-July and then persisting activity until late December. This was attributed to the “super K” strain of H3N2 influenza that has also been circulating this year. Influenza activity does vary between different parts of Australia. Tropical regions tend to get two peaks of influenza each year: one early in the year and a second around the same time as the other states. Why does the influenza season vary from year to year? The drivers of influenza transmission are still unknown, which makes long-term predictions difficult. In general, infectious diseases are an interaction between the “agent” (characteristics of the influenza virus) the “host” (characteristics of the people who are susceptible to influenza) and the environment that brings them together. The influenza virus changes from year to year, and each strain may have different properties, such as being able spread more readily, or to cause more severe disease. Apart from pandemics due to completely new strains, seasonal influenza is usually a small variation on the previously circulating strain. So most people have some degree of at least partial immunity to influenza, which may also be enhanced by vaccination. People’s behaviour can also impact influenza transmission. An obvious example is school holidays reducing transmission in school-aged children. The role of the environment is less clear with influenza, but it is likely some combinations of temperature and humidity may increase the spread. What else can cause flu-like illnesses? Influenza is not the only virus that causes flu-like symptoms. Other viruses such as rhinovirus can cause flu-like symptoms, but less commonly cause serious illness. However, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – and since 2020 SARS-CoV-2, the cause of COVID – can also cause significant illness. The pattern of RSV has been similar to previous years, and COVID activity continues to decline. What about influenza vaccines? Influenza vaccines are partially protective against influenza, and the degree of protection can vary year to year. Preliminary data this year suggests the influenza vaccine reduces the risk of hospitalisation with severe influenza by about 35%. This is on the lower side when compared to estimates in previous years. The proportion of people who get a vaccine varies by age group. In older people (65 and over), around 60% of people have received an influenza vaccine this year, down from around 70% in 2022. In pre-school children (aged 2–5 years), 28% have received a flu vaccine, similar to the figures reported in 2022. What does the unusual influenza season mean for me? The unusual pattern of influenza means it’s still worth getting an influenza vaccine now, if you haven’t had one earlier this year. Although there is some evidence that the protection from influenza vaccine does wane over three to six months, people vaccinated early in the season still have some protection. A second vaccine in the same season is generally not recommended. (The exceptions to this are young children who have not previously received an influenza vaccine, and people with specific conditions such as those receiving bone marrow transplants.) The influenza vaccine is free for high-risk groups including older people, young children and people with chronic medical illnesses. Talk to your pharmacist, GP, nurse or Aboriginal health practitioner. Influenza vaccines may also be available through workplace immunisation programs. Read more: Can I get a free flu shot? (Freepik) JAKARTA - Influenza is often considered a mild disease that is quite manageable with rest and treatment at home. In fact, in certain groups, including children, influenza infection can develop into a more serious disease and trigger complications. One of the preventive measures that can be taken is regular influenza vaccination. The Indonesian Pediatric Association (IDAI) recommends influenza vaccination every year for children starting at six months of age. The vaccine is intended to help reduce the risk of infection and reduce the possibility of severe illness and complications due to influenza. "Influenza vaccination must be given every year because the influenza virus continues to evolve through antigenic drift and antigenic shift. This year's vaccine is designed to match the strains predicted to circulate," said IDAI Tropical Disease Infection Coordination Working Group Member Prof. Dr. Anggraini Alam, Sp.A, Subsp IPT(K), as quoted by ANTARA, Monday, September 21. According to Anggraini, vaccination in children not only provides protection for children who receive the vaccine. This effort can also help protect other family members, especially infants under six months of age who have not been able to get the flu vaccine. Currently, influenza vaccines are available in several types, namely trivalent or quadrivalent inactivated vaccines and intranasal live vaccines that can be given to healthy individuals aged 2-49 years. Vaccination is also said to reduce the risk of infection by about 40 to 60 percent while helping to reduce the severity of the disease and complications. The vaccination recommendation comes as influenza activity in the Southeast Asian region shows an increase. Based on data from the World Health Organization (WHO) published through the WHO Western Pacific Region for the period 1 September 2025 to 30 August 2026, influenza activity in the Southeast Asia region continues to increase. Meanwhile, monitoring through the sentinel system in Indonesia shows positive influenza activity that fluctuates throughout the year. The peak of activity was recorded at the end of 2025, then there was an increase again in mid-2026. The Indonesian Ministry of Health also reported that the subtype of Influenza A H3N2 subklad K has been detected in 13 provinces. An increase in the number of patients due to influenza was also reported in East Java. Children are one of the groups that need attention when influenza activity increases. The Secretary General of the IDAI Central Board, DR Dr Hikari Ambara Sjakti, Sp.A, Subsp H.Onk(K) said that children are a group that is vulnerable to influenza infection. "Global data show that children aged 0-17 years have a two-fold higher risk of experiencing symptomatic influenza infection than adults," said Hikari. He explained that children's immune systems are still naive so that their bodies are not strong enough to immediately control the impact of viral infections. Children also tend to release more and longer amounts of virus, potentially becoming a source of transmission in the family and school environment. IDAI data shows that about five percent of children infected with influenza require hospitalization. Of these, about 80 percent are children under two years of age, while 50 percent are under six months of age. Vaccination is not the only way to reduce the risk of influenza transmission. IDAI also reminds the importance of implementing a number of simple habits in daily life, such as washing hands regularly, using masks when necessary, implementing cough etiquette, and not bringing sick children to school or playgrounds until their condition recovers. Children who are infected with influenza can also transmit the virus from about 24 hours before symptoms appear to 10 days later. Therefore, when children have influenza, parents are advised to ensure that children get enough rest, meet fluid needs, and give fever-reducing drugs as indicated. For patients who are at high risk or have severe symptoms, treatment according to the doctor's prescription can be given with a dose adjusted to age and weight. This treatment is ideally carried out within the first 48 hours after symptoms appear. Parents also need to recognize the signs that require immediate medical attention. Shortness of breath, high fever that does not go down, decreased consciousness, to dehydration are a number of dangerous signs that need to be aware of. If these symptoms appear, the child should be taken to the nearest health facility immediately. Prev Next By: Jessica Roe Posted 10:52 AM, Sep 17, 2026 and last updated 6:44 PM, Sep 17, 2026 The 2026-27 COVID vaccine is now available on the Central Coast, arriving just as health officials confirm they've already detected a new strain of the virus in California. The San Luis Obispo County Public Health Department says the Pfizer 12+ and Moderna vaccines arrived this week, and both will be available as of Thursday. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Interim Health Officer Dr. Rick Rosen said the virus is showing up in wastewater data across the state, signaling what he describes as a late-summer, early-fall peak. "This year, it looks like there's a late summer, early fall peak," Rosen said. Rosen said the Food and Drug Administration recently approved the 2026-27 COVID vaccine, which was the final step needed before doses could be distributed in San Luis Obispo County. The flu vaccine is also now available locally. KSBY COVID vaccines arrive as has COVID in California "We don't really have a sense of what kind of a season we'll see. Meaning how many cases we'll see, how severe illnesses will be," Rosen said. San Luis Obispo County health officials say they expect both COVID-19 and influenza to continue circulating this fall and winter. The county monitors local wastewater, test positivity rates and other indicators to track respiratory virus activity, including COVID-19, influenza and RSV. Why get vaccinated? According to Rosen, COVID-19 no longer causes the same level of disruption seen during the height of the pandemic, but it continues to cause hospitalizations and deaths, particularly among older adults and people with underlying health conditions. He said the primary benefit of vaccination is reducing the risk of severe disease, hospitalization, and death, and that while vaccination does not guarantee someone will avoid infection, it can make an infection less likely to become severe. The 2026-27 COVID vaccine has been updated to target strains currently circulating, rather than the original 2020 virus. The 2026-27 flu vaccine is trivalent, meaning it targets three influenza viruses: an H1N1 virus, an H3N2 virus and an influenza B/Victoria lineage virus. All three components were updated for this season, with the H3N2 component targeting the XFG variant. The California Department of Public Health urges residents to get both vaccines. A graphic below from the West Coast Health Alliance outlines the recommendations in detail: KSBY and the West Coast Health Alliance West Coast Health Alliance 2026-2027 Vaccine Recommendations The West Coast Health Alliance recommends the COVID vaccine for all infants six to 23 months old, children ages two to 18 with risk factors or who have never been vaccinated, those in contact with high-risk individuals, those planning a pregnancy, everyone over 65, and all healthcare workers. The alliance also recommends the flu vaccine for everyone over six months old. What residents are saying Not everyone is on the same page about getting vaccinated this season. Diana and Kent Bittleston said they plan to get their vaccines and have no hesitation about doing so. "No vaccine fatigue; we always get our vaccines and flu shots, we just haven't gotten them yet," they said. Ismail Karabulut said he believes vaccination is important and shared a personal experience that reinforced that view. "I think everyone should get vaccinated. I don't think there should be any fatigue around it. In the past there was one year I forgot to get the flu and I got extremely sick and it's something I'm never going to do again," Karabulut said. Steve and Sandra Marshall said they plan to get both vaccines. "Well, we're definitely going to get both of them, flu and COVID," they said. Others are less certain. Diana Ash said she got the COVID vaccine when it first became available but has since had second thoughts. "I did get it when it first came out, and I'm finding out now that they're saying that is not good, so I'm kind of like on the border of not getting one this year," Ash said. Patricia Margolis said she has decided not to get vaccinated. "My individual decision is that nothing should be shot inside the body," Margolis said. Nationwide vaccination rates remain low Despite the recommendations, nationwide vaccination rates remain low. According to Centers for Disease Control data, only 18% of adults received a COVID vaccine last season, and only about 46% got a flu shot. A University of Michigan poll of adults 50 and older found nearly three in 10 said they skipped the vaccine simply because they do not think they need it. Insurance and access In California, vaccines recommended by the California Department of Public Health continue to be covered by health insurance regulated in the state. COVID vaccines are expected to be covered by most insurance plans, including Medi-Cal, and flu vaccines are generally covered as well. Residents are encouraged to check with their health plan or provider regarding their specific coverage and where they can receive the vaccine. For people without insurance or who are underinsured, programs and community providers may offer vaccines at low or no cost, depending on eligibility. News Football Celebs PRIVACY Flu 'super K' strain already in UK causes surge in Australia - symptoms Flu season down under usually gives advanced warning of what will hit the UK - and strain is 'highly infectious' The UK could be hit by 'Super K' flu this winter(Getty) By Ben Hurst 15:23, 18 Sep 2026 A virulent strain of flu has surged in Australia in an ‘unusual’ wave, meaning the UK could be bracing itself for a bad season. Every year, the Australian flu season - usually until August provides an important indicator of what the UK may face in the following winter. However the country is currently in the grip of an epidemic - with high rates of infection. In the fortnight ending September 6, the Australian Respiratory Surveillance report recorded 31,650 notified influenza cases, up 27.2% from the previous period, according to figures just released. Infections have risen by 25% in Victoria over the past six weeks, primarily driven by children aged 5 to 17 years. Chief health officer, Dr Caroline McElnay, said the flu season ‘has arrived later than in previous years, with cases continuing to rise as we move into spring.’ She said people could “protect themselves and their loved ones these school holidays by staying home when sick, keeping unwell children at home, and reminding everyone that it’s not too late to get a flu vaccine”. Experts said a ‘Super-K’ strain which has already been detected in the UK is said to be spreading in a number of waves. It is also know as the ‘Super-K strain’ or a ‘super flu’. The Uk Health Security Agency said: “Subclade K is the variant of influenza A (H3N2) that dominated last flu season (2025-26) in the UK. We saw flu activity both start and decline early last year and although K strain was the dominant strain, there is no evidence that it caused particularly severe illness in those who caught it.“ It said the Subclade K is one of the strains the flu vaccine offers protection against. Super-K is said to be highly transmissible. CONTINUE READING What are the symptoms of Super-K flu? The symptoms of Super-K infection are very similar to those of regular influenza and include: Fever and chills Cough and sore throat Runny or blocked nose Headache Muscle and joint aches Extreme tiredness and fatigue Doctors On Demand Australia said: “The H3N2 subclade K / Super-K flu variant is a reminder that influenza viruses continually evolve, and that vigilance matters. While there’s no evidence it causes more severe illness than other variants, its high transmissibility has made for an unusually strong flu season.” Dr James McCaw, an epidemiologist at the University of Melbourne’s Infectious Disease Dynamics Unit, confirmed the timing of the 2026 flu season was “definitely late” compared with typical winter peaks. He said: “We don’t understand enough about influenza biology and epidemiology to know exactly why that might be the case. It’s unusual, but ... it doesn’t make it more severe or more mild, it’s just late,” Queensland’s chief health officer, Dr Marianne Gale, said this “more unusual flu season” may be due to last year’s record cases. “In addition to that, we also had a second wave of the ‘Super-K’ strain from Europe throughout December and January,” she said in a statement last month. “These factors change the population’s immunity to flu, which is likely why we’re seeing a different looking flu season this year.” Who is eligible for the flu vaccine this year? From September 1 2026, the following groups are eligible. Where ‘clinical risk groups’ are mentioned, these are defined in the Green Book, Influenza Chapter: pregnant women all children aged 2 or 3 years on 31 August 2026 primary school and secondary school-aged children, from reception to year 11 young people aged 17 and over attending a special educational needs (SEN) school who are also in a clinical risk group all children in clinical risk groups, from 6 months to less than 18 years Show more From October 1 2026, the following groups become eligible: everyone aged 65 years and over all adults in clinical risk groups, from age 18 to under 65 residents of long-stay residential care homes carers in receipt of carer's allowance, or those who are the main carer of an elderly or disabled person close contacts of people who are immunocompromised rough sleepers and those using homeless hostels or night shelters aged 16 years and over frontline social care workers without access to an employer-led occupational health scheme, including those working in: registered residential care or nursing homes domiciliary care voluntary managed hospices personal assistants employed through direct payments or personal health budgets UKHSA said: "If you're eligible, the NHS will usually contact you to tell you when you can book. For parents of most school-aged children this will be via their school. If you think you're eligible but don’t hear anything, speak to your GP practice, pharmacist, or, if you're pregnant, your midwife. "The best time to get vaccinated is in autumn or early winter, before flu starts spreading widely. If you miss this window, it's still worth getting vaccinated later, as flu activity can continue throughout winter." records.content: 浦江头条 > 感冒发烧的人多起来了?今年流感提前了吗?专家释疑 澎湃新闻首席记者 陈斯斯 2026-09-17 15:39 来源: 澎湃新闻 进入9月,天气逐渐转凉,呼吸道疾病也将迎来高发季。近日,在社交平台上,“最近感冒发烧的人又多起来了”“今年流感是不是提前了”等话题,引起社会关注。 在社交平台上,最近关注“今年流感是否提前”的人群多了起来。 网络 图 针对上述话题,2026年9月17日,上海市第十人民医院急诊科副主任周书琴接受澎湃新闻记者采访时表示,今年6、7月,上海确实出现了一波新型冠状病毒检测阳性率上升的情况,进入7、8月后,新冠病例数逐步回落、明显减少,但流感病例数开始悄然抬头,感染病例正在逐步递增,“往年,流感往往是在10月、11月开始逐步上升,今年从临床情况来看,相对早了一些。” 针对近期流感小幅上升的态势,临床医生呼吁市民及时接种流感疫苗。“流感疫苗接种后,并非即刻起效,往往需要2-4周的时间才能在人体内产生抗体,提前接种能在流感高发期形成有效防护。”周书琴说道。 医院:流感检出率明显升高,甲流为主 “目前,医院甲流、乙流阳性检出率及就诊人数较此前均有明显上升。”周书琴表示,在医院急诊就诊的出现流鼻涕等单纯上呼吸道感染症状的患者中,流感检出率明显升高,且不少同时伴随发烧以及消化道症状如腹泻等。从病毒检出情况来看,现阶段上海流感流行毒株以甲流为主,乙流检出数量相对少些。 上海市儿童医院急诊科主任黄玉娟9月17日也向记者透露,在出现流感样症状的儿童群体中,流感阳性检出率亦有所上升,“但目前还处在流行前期,还未到达秋冬流感高峰。”据介绍,当前季节性流行以甲型 H3N2为主,同时叠加乙型 Victoria 系共同传播,“甲型流感传播速度快,易发生变异,常引发较大范围的流行;乙型流感在儿童中更为多见,不少患儿感染后还会出现呕吐、腹泻等消化道症状。” 在临床检测方面,目前各大医院对流感样症状患者多采用抗原或核酸检测方式。根据上海市儿童医院近期流感检测数据,9月7日至13日,通过抗原检测的1500余例流感样症状病例中,阳性率为12.52%,通过核酸检测的3500余例病例中,阳性率为19.19%。“相比7、8月,9月以来流感阳性检出率有所上升。”黄玉娟表示。 黄玉娟表示,往年流感流行以秋冬季为主,而今年8月份医院甲流检出率约为8%,乙流约为1%-2%。“从医院临床检测数据来说,的确有提前的表现,但后续仍需要密切监测流感动态情况。目前,医院在流感治疗药物配备方面很充足。” 2026年9月17日中午,位于泸定路上的上海市儿童医院急诊,不少家长带着感冒症状的患儿前来就诊。上海市儿童医院 供图 感染流感后,不同年龄人群症状不同 根据中国疾控中心最新发布的2026年第36周(2026年8月31日-9月6日)流感监测数据显示,当前,新型冠状病毒检测阳性率呈下降趋势,总体上已降至低流行水平。流感活动近期小幅上升,主要为B(Victoria)系和A(H3N2)亚型流感病毒,A(H3N2)亚型占比上升,南方省份检测阳性率处于中流行水平,北方省份处于流行间期水平,15-59岁病例组检测阳性率最高。 感染了流感,哪些人群需要注意?周书琴指出,最近在该院急诊中检出流感病毒感染的病例中,老年人不少,主要集中在护理院或养老机构居住的老人,以及居家的老年人群体,“和普通感染者不同的是,这些老人往往不存在典型的高热、明显的上呼吸道感染症状,他们来医院的时候往往是说自己浑身乏力、胃口变差、精神萎靡等,但经检测发现存在流感病毒感染,部分患者已经发展为肺炎等重症,这一类老年患者大多本身患有糖尿病、高血压、脑梗等基础性疾病。” 2026年9月17日上午,在上海市第十人民医院急诊,一名患者正在进行流感病毒的检测。 上海市第十人民医院 供图 周书琴进一步表示,老年患者就诊往往会相对滞后,这样会导致体内流感病毒复制时间长、病毒载量偏高,后续抗病毒治疗效果大打折扣,治疗周期被大幅延长,流感病毒转阴需要耗费更长时间,治疗难度显著增加。 上海市儿童医院急诊科主治医师郭玉哲则表示,不同年龄段的孩子,感染流感病毒后表现出来的状态不一样,0到3岁的小宝宝症状往往不够典型,不一定会有明显咳嗽,只会出现不爱吃饭、频繁哭闹、呼吸急促的现象;3到6岁的孩子发热、咳嗽的感受会更突出,整个人不爱活动;6岁以上的儿童症状就和成人比较接近,高烧不退,浑身酸痛,精神状态明显变差。“大家可以记住一个简单判断的小方法,流感流行期间,如果孩子突然发高烧,喊浑身酸痛,精神状态不好,就要高度怀疑流感,尽快做相关检测。” 2026年9月17日,上海市儿童医院门诊大厅。 近期得过感冒发烧,还有必要打流感疫苗吗? 针对流感活动近期小幅上升的态势,上述临床医生都呼吁市民及时接种流感疫苗。 针对不少市民认为“近期得过感冒发烧,就不用接种流感疫苗”的错误想法,周书琴明确表示,普通感冒、普通发烧并不等同于流感感染,出现过感冒发烧症状,不代表体内已经产生流感病毒抗体,市民依旧存在感染流感病毒的风险,建议这类人群在身体症状完全消失、身体恢复一段时间后,及时接种流感疫苗。 “从临床来看,接种流感疫苗能够显著降低流感重症、并发症的发生概率,对于免疫力较弱人群、患有各类基础性疾病的易感人群而言,接种疫苗是预防流感、规避重症风险最科学、最有效的手段。”周书琴表示。 根据2026年9月2日中国疾病预防控制中心发布的《中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026-2027)》显示,2026-2027年度我国上市的三价流感疫苗包括三价灭活疫苗和三价减毒活疫苗,其中三价灭活疫苗有裂解疫苗和亚单位疫苗,可用于6月龄及以上人群,包括 0.25mL和0.5 mL两种剂型;三价减毒活疫苗适用于3-17岁人群,每剂次 0.2 mL。 值得注意的是,上述指南明确:对于6月龄及以上-9岁以下儿童,若该年龄段儿童既往未接种过流感疫苗,首次接种流感病毒灭活疫苗时,应接种2剂次(2剂次选择同一厂家同种疫苗),间隔≥4周;若该年龄段儿童既往接种过流感疫苗,则本年度建议接种1剂次。若该年龄段儿童接种流感病毒减毒活疫苗,无论既往是否接种过流感疫苗,仅需接种1剂次。对于9岁及以上儿童和成人,无论既往是否接种过流感疫苗,仅需接种1剂次。 上述指南明确,综合我国南、北方的流感流行特点,通常在11月份左右进入冬春季流感流行季,建议在 9-10 月完成接种;即使此时间段内未完成接种,整个流行季也都可以接种。 责任编辑: 郑浩 图片编辑: 沈轲 校对: 丁晓 54 评论 霸道总裁 建议直接公布各大医院检测出来的病毒排行,比说一千道一万都管用。 4天前 ∙ 河北 17赞 弋麻 别一发烧就往流感上套,吓自己最在行。 4天前 ∙ 广东 13赞 衣画谢华华 其实就是普通感冒,早睡早起多喝水比啥都强。 4天前 ∙ 四川 展开更多评论 相关推荐 共赴技能之约,同筑匠心之基——写在第48届世界技能大赛开幕之际 浦江头条 10分钟前 1 上海街头的“慢镜头”:所有车辆为何为一个老人按下“暂停键” 浦江头条 10小时前 21评 上海市政府常务会议传达学习习近平总书记关于发展先进制造业的重要指示精神,研究做好三季度经济社会发展各项工作 浦江头条 11小时前 近300项首发首秀,第26届工博会将于10月12日在沪开幕 浦江头条 11小时前 24小时最热 广东省人大常委会党组成员覃伟中被查,曾任深圳市长 打虎记 14小时前 69评 咸阳一新生儿遭月子中心护工拍打案一审裁定:涉嫌虐待,移送公安 一号专案 11小时前 59评 张又侠、刘振立严重违纪违法被开除党籍军籍 中国政库 13小时前 100评 重庆理工大学通报“廖某被我校原教师李某性侵后报警未立案” 直击现场 10小时前 59评 贾国龙:结合西贝惨痛的教训,恳请进一步厘清高流量网络账号的言论边界 10%公司 17小时前 401评 你有权知道更多 下载澎湃新闻客户端 下载APP 山西明长城损毁事件调查:被持续损毁近二十载,为何无人追究 咸阳一新生儿遭月子中心护工拍打案一审裁定:涉嫌虐待,移送公安 重庆理工大学通报“廖某被我校原教师李某性侵后报警未立案” 大牌平替,“蹭”来的好生意?|湃客Talk
